edges.effect_quant: Across occupation-focused meta-analyses, hairdressing work is associated with a modest excess in bladder-cancer risk, with the strongest signal seen in longer-duration exposure.
edges.mechanism: Hairdressing can involve repeated dermal and inhalational exposure to aromatic amines, dyes, and other salon chemicals that have long been scrutinized in bladder-carcinogenesis research. The plausible exposure pathway matters here more than any single modern product, because the epidemiology reflects cumulative occupational contact over years.
edges.summary: The most direct pooled analysis found that bladder-cancer risk is elevated in hairdressers, and the broader occupation-level meta-analyses point in the same direction. This is not a giant effect, but it is one of the more reproducible occupation-specific bladder-cancer signals rather than an isolated statistical blip.
edges.caveats: Risk likely varies by era, product formulation, glove use, ventilation, and years worked. Much of the literature pools older cohorts, so the edge should be read as a modest long-term occupational risk signal, not as proof that current salon practice carries the same magnitude of harm everywhere.
